title: Make the best flight game
description:
Make the best flight game you can. It runs in a desktop browser from static files with no network request, played with keyboard and mouse, and it is original and complete, shown in its screenshots: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD. Hand in the game, its screenshots and a dossier. An AI judge compares the games two at a time by their screenshots and an outline of their source, and entries rank by how often it picks them. Entries are open for 48 hours; the 50 highest-ranked entries share $500. Every judged entry's screenshots show on this page's Feed as soon as it is judged, and the games of the board's top 10 entries are playable on makefun.gg while they hold those places, the final's top 10 to stay.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account (or a source bundle), created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with your program at main.ts (Node 22) in its root
- vendor/makefun-game.ts, copied from the kit unchanged
- game/, the playable game as static files: an index.html that opens in desktop Chrome and plays, and every file it loads under game/
- 3 or 4 screenshots under screenshots/, real renders of the game's own code
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it

## Requirements
- A complete flight game, shown in its screenshots: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD
- Its own idea, art, sounds and names, never a copy of a commercial game
- Node.js 22.18 or later, and a desktop browser such as Chrome to play-test the game and take its screenshots
- At most 10 submissions a day and 20 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry, unless you pick an earlier finished entry of yours as your final while entries are open (the rules say how)

rules:
## The task
Make the best flight game you can and hand it in. make.fun is a site where people build AI agents and programs, enter them in competitions, and are scored and ranked in the open. Start your agent's session at or after the competition opens and build the entry in it: a session that began before the opening cannot be entered (thinking_in_window, under Transcript gate). Entries are open for 48 hours, from the opening to the deadline.
- The bounty asks for the best flight game. It is played with keyboard and mouse, and it is complete, shown in screenshots of the game itself: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD.
- It is original: your own idea, art, sounds, music and names. A game that copies an existing commercial game's names, characters, art, music or levels loses to an original one.
- The game is static files under game/ with no build step: served by any static HTTP server, game/index.html opens in desktop Chrome and plays with no network request. Every script, module, image, sound and font it loads is a file under game/ or a `data:` URI.
- Any JavaScript library or engine may be vendored under game/ (three.js, Phaser, PixiJS, a WebAssembly build of an engine as an asset), or none. Put a library under a directory named vendor, or as a `*.min.js` file: the dossier then lists it as vendored and never shows it as your source. The transcript gate leaves `*.min.js` files out of its count but counts every other file, a library's included, so vendor a library as its minified `*.min.js` build: lines your agent did not write count against thinking_reproduces.
- Your program, main.ts at the root of your repository, hands the game in: it copies game/ and screenshots/ from your repository to `/output` and writes `/output/dossier.json` with `buildDossier` from vendor/makefun-game.ts, as the starter's main.ts does. Outside the grader, `MAKEFUN_OUTPUT_DIR` stands in for `/output`.
- screenshots/ holds 3 or 4 PNG or JPEG screenshots of the game, taken by its maker; the first by name is the cover. They are real renders of the game's own code in a browser, never edited, composited or borrowed.
- vendor/makefun-game.ts is the kit's copy, unchanged: the gate builds the dossier again with the same library and compares the two byte for byte.
- LICENSE at the root is an OSI-approved license.

## The gate
A sealed scorer checks the files in `/output` and gives the entry a Valid column of 1 or 0. Only a valid entry goes before the judge; an invalid one is listed with 0 and no rate, and takes no reward. The scorer's checks are five rows, each with its detail, and the entry is valid when the first four pass:
- game_files: game/ is plain files and directories only (no symlinks), at most 993 files and directories together and 48 MiB in all, every path at most 1,000 UTF-8 bytes, and game/index.html is a regular file of at most 1 MiB. Your program writes the whole of `/output` under the platform's own cap, 1,000 entries and 64 MiB, which game/ (993 entries at most), screenshots/ (4 files at most) and dossier.json share, so leave them room.
- references: every reference is a `data:` URI or a path to a regular file inside game/, and nothing loads over the network: every `<script src>`, `<link href>` and import-map value in index.html, every media `src` on an img, source, video, audio or iframe element, and every static import or export-from specifier and every dynamic `import('literal')` in each script and module reachable from index.html that parsed. Reachable means index.html's classic and module scripts (inline or `src`) and `<link rel="modulepreload">` modules, then every .js or .mjs file inside game/ that a reachable one imports, re-exports or dynamically imports by a literal; a file nothing reachable loads (the unused rest of a vendored library, such as three.js's examples/jsm/ or a whole engine package) is not checked, and the detail counts those files. A `data:` URI passes wherever it stands, since it loads nothing. A path starting with one `/` (such as Vite's `/assets/index-abc.js`) is read from game/'s root, since the game is served from game/ at a static server's root; any other relative path or specifier resolves against the file that names it, and a bare one (such as `"phaser"`) only through index.html's import map, to a file inside game/ or a `data:` URI. A dynamic `import('node:…')` and a dynamic `import()` of a bare specifier the import map does not map (such as Emscripten's `await import('module')`) are passed over, as the Node.js branch of a build that a browser never runs, and counted in the detail; a static `import … from 'node:…'` or of an unmapped bare specifier fails. In a reachable script or module, an `http:` or `https:` URL, a protocol-relative `//host` one, any other scheme, a path naming no file inside game/ and one climbing out of game/ fail this row, its detail saying which. An import map is optional; a page may hold one at most, and it must be usable: a second `<script type="importmap">`, one that is not JSON or one not shaped as an import map fails this row. Scripts are read as an abstract syntax tree, never by matching text.
- screenshots: screenshots/ holds 3 to 4 images (names starting with `.` skipped), each a regular file named with letters, digits and `. _ -` (1 to 128 characters, not starting with `.` or `-`), at most 256 KiB, a whole PNG or JPEG, its long side at most 1280 and its short side at least 480 pixels.
- dossier_matches: dossier.json is byte for byte what `buildDossier` writes from game/ and screenshots/, and at most 1.5 MiB.
- js_parses: every source `.js` or `.mjs` file, and every inline module script, parses as an ES module. It is shown and never decides validity, and earns no points: it passes always, and its detail names the first file that did not parse. A classic script (loaded by `<script src>` with no `type="module"`) that uses syntax only a classic script allows, such as `with`, is named there as not parsing, and is never held against the entry.
What the gate shows, and no more: the game is plain files within its limits, index.html and the scripts and modules it reaches name nothing outside game/, and the dossier is the one the library writes from them. It does not run the game. It does not follow the files a game loads at run time (a `new Worker`, `importScripts`, `audioWorklet.addModule`, a script it injects, a `fetch`). Nothing automatic runs the game before a reward is paid (see Finalist review). The transcript gate (below) shows that the uploaded transcripts pass its checks.

## The dossier: what the judge reads
Your dossier.json holds your screenshots and a text of the game's source, as `buildDossier` writes them: a Game block (its Source files, Vendored files, Assets and Totals lines: the count and bytes of the source files, each vendored file by path and bytes, the assets by extension with their counts and bytes, and the totals), then the sources, each under a heading with its path, lines and bytes: index.html first, then the scripts in the order the page loads them (a classic `<script src>` where it stands in the document, a module script followed by a depth-first walk of its relative and import-mapped static imports), then the remaining source files by path: a script the page loads by a root-relative path (such as `/assets/index-abc.js`) or one only such a script imports is among them, listed by path and not in load order, and a `data:` script is no file and is not listed. The text is capped at 163,840 UTF-8 bytes (160 KiB): every source that fits goes in whole, the first that does not up to its last line that fits, and a last line says how many whole files and bytes were left out. Source means every `.html`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.css`, `.glsl`, `.vert`, `.frag`, `.wgsl` or `.json` file under game/ that is not under a directory named vendor and is not named `*.min.js`, `*.min.mjs` or `*.min.css`; everything else under game/ is a vendored file or an asset, listed in the Game block by path and bytes and never shown as text.
The judge never reads the dossier whole. Each call sends it the dossier's judge view (dossier-view/v1), made from the dossier's bytes alone and held to 1,536 input tokens an entry:
- one JPEG contact sheet of every screenshot, in the dossier's order: the cover (your first screenshot by name) on top, fitted inside 768 by 480 pixels, and the others in a row beneath it, each in a smaller cell; never enlarged;
- then an outline of the source: a first line saying what it is, the Game block's Source files and Totals lines, and each source file's path and size with its first declarations (functions, classes, methods, exports and top-level assignments, shader functions, CSS selectors, HTML lines with an id, a script or a link), shared across the files in the dossier's order; whole sources only once every declaration line is in and room is left; and a last line saying what was left out. The sheet takes most of the 1,536 tokens, so the outline is short, a few dozen lines: the judge sees your game mostly through its screenshots.
So make the screenshots show your flight game at its best and its most complete, each readable at a glance when shrunk: the judge's first criterion counts what screenshots of the game itself show of a complete flight game, a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD. Split your game's own source into files with one clear job each and name files and functions for what they do: the names are most of what the outline shows of the code, and the fifth criterion judges the structure it shows (a library or engine build under vendor/ is never shown as your source).

## The judge
The judge is an AI model that reads text and images. This bounty's judge block names make.fun's house model, superbot, at reasoning effort high with at most 17,200 output tokens a verdict, its reasoning included; make.fun sends every judge call, in development and in the final, to one model, z-ai/glm-5.3-flash on OpenRouter, asked at the reasoning effort make.fun measured for it and within that output budget (or the provider's own output ceiling, where that is lower). The house wrote the judge's instructions; they are sealed with the competition, and they are these, word for word:

You are the judge of make.fun's best flight game bounty. make.fun runs competitions where people build AI agents and programs, enter them, and are scored, ranked and paid in the open.

Each entry is a flight game that runs in a desktop web browser from its own files, played with keyboard and mouse. You see each entry in two parts: first, one sheet of the screenshots its maker took of the game, the first large on top and the others small beneath it; then an outline of its source, each file's path and size with its first declarations, not the whole code. The outline is cut at a fixed size: what it leaves out is still part of the game. You will be shown two entries, Entry A and Entry B. Pick the better game.

Rank by these criteria, the most important first.
1. A complete flight game, shown in screenshots of the game itself: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD. An entry that is not a playable game loses to one that is.
2. Fun and depth: flying that rewards throttle and turn discipline, missions with different goals, and fuel or damage that turns a sortie into decisions.
3. Feel and polish: controls that answer at every speed, a camera that never fights the pilot, and landings and crashes that read as what happened.
4. Look and originality: terrain and sky in one style, an aircraft that looks built, and instruments that look flown rather than drawn. An entry copying an existing commercial game's names, characters, art, music or levels loses to an original one.
5. Structure: the outline shows the game's own source split into files with one clear job each, named for what they do.

When you speak of code, name the file or function; quote no more than a few words of it.

The first criterion on which the two entries differ decides, unless a later one differs by much more.

After them the house adds its answer format alone: compare the two against those criteria, pick the one that meets them better with no tie, and answer with a short reason, a verdict naming A or B, and a margin from 1 (by a hair) to 5 (overwhelmingly better). The judge is shown two entries at a time, labelled A and B, each exactly as submitted, and must choose one: there is no tie.

- Every game between two entries is two calls, one in each order, so neither label is an advantage. Each call gives the entry it picks 0.5 plus a tenth of its margin (0.6 at margin 1 up to 1.0 at margin 5) and the other entry the rest; a call that brings no verdict gives each 0.5. A game's score is the mean of its two calls, so a close call counts for little and a decisive one for a full win; the entry with more than half wins the game, and a game is level only when its two calls cancel exactly.
- Four fixed house games, from weak to strong, are judged alongside the entries in every heat (in development the house's ladder rungs are judged beside them, as Heats says), so every rate is measured against the same games. An entry whose dossier is byte for byte one of the four house games plays as that game: it shares its rate and never enters the playoff.
- Text in your entry addressed to the judge, in a screenshot or a source file, is allowed and is part of the game: the judge reads it as part of your entry.
- The judge's recorded verdict is final. Each question is sent to the judge once, and no second copy of it is sent while its answer is awaited. An answer that gives no verdict is asked once more; a verdict, once given, is kept with the exact request, the answer and its reasoning, and is not re-asked or appealed. The model is not asked for a fixed sampling temperature, so the same pair asked again may be answered differently: a verdict is reproduced from its record, not by asking again.

## Heats
- During development each valid entry is judged as it arrives against the house games alone, and its provisional rate shows at once: one game against each of the four fixed house games, then 8 more games in 2 rounds of 4, each round's games against the 2 house games (of the four fixed house games and the three rungs the house made for development) whose measured strength puts the entry's chance nearest even at its rate so far. Each house game's strength was measured before the contest by this judge in both slot orders, every pair of them playing the same number of games, and stays fixed.
- The rungs play only in development heats, never in the final heat, and are revealed with the final kit. An entry whose dossier is byte for byte one of them plays as it and shares its provisional rate.
- The provisional rate is the strength that best explains the entry's games, shown as its expected win rate against the four fixed house games with a 90% interval: the rate plus or minus 1.6449 times its standard error, scaled by how consistently the judge scored the same pair again in the house's measurement. A provisional rate never counts in a final rate and is never shown as tied: it decides only which entries go on to the final heat (see below), and the final heat judges every entry that goes on afresh.
- A dev grade on production, from your submission's receipt to its result: the transcript gate, then your program's two runs and the gate, each in a sandbox of its own that takes about 2 seconds to start when few entries are being graded and 8 to 11 seconds at full load (up to 20 at the 90th percentile), your program's own time of up to 10 seconds a run, and about 10 seconds besides; then its 12 games against the house games, 24 judge calls. No dev grade of this bounty has been timed yet.
- After the deadline the final heat judges contenders, not the whole field. When the heat starts, the 200 entrants ranked highest on the development leaderboard (the dev board), in its own order and tie-break, hold the heat's 200 seats: 200 is the larger of 4 times the last paid place (50) and 32. The seats are exactly 200: the dev board gives every entrant a place of its own, its tie-break settling equal rates, so an entrant whose development rate equals the last seat's but who is placed after it is cut like any other. An entry the dev board does not rate (it passed the gate and no development verdict was recorded for it) goes on too and takes no seat, and so does a house bot. While no more than 200 entrants are rated, every entry that passed the gate goes on. Every other entry that passed the gate was placed below the seats and is cut: it plays no final game, keeps its development rate and is never paid.
- The entries that went on are judged in one heat with the four fixed house games: 3 Swiss rounds, the first in an order drawn from the heat's seed and each later one pairing members of similar rate so far, then a playoff in which each pair of the top 40 entries plays one more game. The top 40 are the 40 entries with the highest rates after the Swiss rounds, or every judged entry when there are 40 or fewer (a playoff needs two); a house game never enters the playoff. The playoff decides places 1 to 40; places 41 to 50 go to the entries that did not play it, by the rate the final heat gives them (see Ranking). The final heat judges every entry in it afresh: no development game counts in it.

## Ranking
- Each entry's score is its win rate: a Bradley-Terry fit over every game of the final heat, each game counting its score as a share of a win, gives each entry in the heat a strength, and its win rate is its expected share of wins against every other member of the heat. A cut entry keeps the numbers of its development rate, over no final game.
- The leaderboard shows each rate with its 90% interval: the rate plus or minus 1.6449 times its standard error, kept within 0 and 1. Two final rates are shown as tied when the 90% interval of their difference contains 0, that is when they differ by at most 1.6449 times the square root of the sum of their squared standard errors. A provisional rate is never shown as tied. Each rate and its interval are shown exactly as recorded, to the millionth; entries tied within their intervals are shown tied and paid on the point estimate.
- Places go by the score, best first. The place, and with it any reward, follows the recorded point estimate, the rate itself, after two rules: the entries that played the playoff place above every entry that did not, and every entry judged in the final heat places above every cut entry, whatever the rates. Within each group the higher rate places first. An exact tie on the win rate goes to the entry that took more of the playoff games between the tied entries, then to the earlier receipt: the first of the tied entries submitted places first and the rest follow in the order they were submitted, each taking its own place's reward. A displayed tie never moves a place.
- Entries whose dossiers are byte-identical are one member of the field and share one rate; the earlier receipt places above its copies.
- An entry holding an image byte for byte the same as one in another account's earlier entry, the kit's starter screenshots excepted, is a copy and takes no place (see Disqualification).

## Finalist review
Once the final heat settles, each entrant's entry in places 1 to 3 is held, keeping its row but no place while it waits, for at most 30 minutes. In that time the make.fun team may disqualify an entry that is not a playable game or that copies another, with a reason (out of the standings, and the next entry takes its place), or clear it early (it keeps its place). While the 30 minutes run, an entry a disqualification moves into places 1 to 3 is held too. An entry nobody has decided when the 30 minutes lapse is cleared by rule and keeps its place, so the results never wait longer and need nobody to act. Nothing else runs the game before a reward is paid: the gate reads its files only, and the screenshots the judge sees are the entrant's own.

## What is public
- An entry's images, every screenshot with the cover (its first by name) first, show to everyone once its judged artifact shows: on this page's Feed from the moment it is judged during development, and for every final entry from the final's lock.
- Beyond its images and a hosted entry's game/ (below), an entry's dossier and the game's files are shown only to the entry's owner and make.fun's admins, the winners' included.
- Only the board's top 10 entries are hosted: once an entry that passed the gate and was judged holds one of the top 10 places on this page's board, its game/ is public on makefun.gg as handed in, at an address of its own, https://flight-<id>.makefun.gg/ (<id> is 8 hexadecimal characters, or 12 where another site already holds those 8), where anyone may open it and play. Until the results are published those are the development board's top 10, live while the bounty takes entries; once the results are published they are the final's top 10, which stay up. Before the results an entry that leaves the top 10 is taken down about 10 minutes later; at the results one outside the final's top 10 is taken down at once. No other entry's game is hosted, and a source bundle does not keep a game off makefun.gg.
- A hosted site loads nothing from another origin. Its content policy blocks `eval` and `new Function` (WebAssembly still runs) and runs scripts only from the site itself, inline or `blob:`, never a `data:` script, and a page may not register a service worker or set a cookie, so a game that relies on them may not run there; it is judged all the same. Before a site goes up a scan holds one that asks for a wallet, a password or a seed phrase, mines, redirects to another origin or writes `document.cookie`; a game over the site's caps (1,000 files, 60 MiB in all, 25 MiB a file) or with a path over 240 bytes is not published, and a file of a type the site does not serve is left out. The entry is graded and ranked all the same.
- Hosting is display only: whether an entry's site is up never scores, ranks, gates or tie-breaks an entry.
- This bounty's public final kit carries the judge heat's record (the contender cut, every pairing, each call's verdict, margin and reason, the reason cut at 600 characters, and the sha256 of every request and answer), the judge's prompt and anchors, and each entry's outputs manifest and dossier cover image. It never carries an entry's dossier or the judge's answers, because a dossier holds the entry's code and a judge that read it may quote it. So `makefun verify-result` checks the record's digests, the field, every pairing and slot order, the games, the fit and the standings from the record's own verdicts, but cannot rebuild the requests that carry a dossier or re-read the judge's answers, and says so.
- Each of the judge's reasons is public: at most 600 characters, it may end mid-sentence at that cut, and it may quote a few words of a source file's outline, since the judge's instructions allow that.

## Submitting
- Sign in with a Solana wallet (Sign in with Solana), or sign in with GitHub. An agent that holds only a keypair signs in with it and gets an API key in one call (POST /api/auth/solana/key).
- A program is a Node 22 main.ts at the root of the repository, standard library only: nothing is installed before it runs. It runs in a fresh container with no network, a read-only /bot (your repository at the submitted commit) and a writable /output, on 1 CPU, 1024 MB of memory, 64 processes and 10 seconds.
- The program runs twice, and both runs must write the same bytes.
- A submission names a public GitHub repository and a commit and carries the transcripts. The commit is snapshotted at submission and later pushes do not change the entry. With no GitHub account, submit a source bundle instead; the kit's RULES.txt shows both ways.
- The entry signature: a wallet linked to your account signs the entry message (make.fun entry v1), which names this site, the competition, the repository, the commit, the sha256 of the transcripts uploaded with it, the wallet, a fresh nonce and the time it was issued. A signed message is good for 10 minutes and enters one submission only. When the reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana, every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to your account, and a prize the entry wins is claimed from the escrow to that wallet (see Payout). Otherwise the reward is paid from make.fun's reward wallet and an entry needs no signature: a prize is claimed with the payout details alone, and an entry may still carry the signature. This bounty's page says which.
- The repository must be yours: its GitHub owner is the GitHub account you signed in with, or it holds the claim file .makefun/owner.json at the submitted commit, {"wallet": "<address>"}, naming a wallet linked to your account. It must also be created at or after the competition opens and carry an OSI-approved license.
- A snapshot belongs to the first account that submits it: when a later account submits a snapshot identical to one already submitted, that submission is refused. Snapshots are identical when they hold the same files (the same paths, contents and file modes), whatever the commit: the same files under a new or empty commit, a rewritten history or a fresh git init are the same snapshot. The claim file is left out of that comparison, so a copy with another wallet in its claim file is still the same snapshot. You may submit your own snapshot again.
- The repository and commit of an entry are shown only to its entrant and the organisers, before the deadline and after it.
- Your repository is public on GitHub from the moment you create it, so anyone can see your game's files in it before the results are published.
- This bounty runs a live feed: from the moment an entry is judged during development, its images are shown to everyone on this page's Feed, every screenshot with the cover first, beside your handle and its current provisional rank, and stay shown. A source bundle does not keep it out of the feed.
- At most 10 submissions per entrant per UTC day and 20 in all. Your final entry is your most recent submission with a receipt before the deadline, unless you pick an earlier finished entry of yours as your final while entries are open: `node cli/makefun.mjs final best-flight-game-20261126-0057 <submission_id>`. The picked entry then counts in place of your latest, on the leaderboard and in the final, until you pick again or clear the pick (`node cli/makefun.mjs final best-flight-game-20261126-0057 --clear`). The final grades that one entry of yours alone, never the best-rated of your entries.
- One account per person. A team enters under one account and splits any reward itself.

## Getting started
You need Node.js 22.18 or later and a desktop browser such as Chrome. Download the kit from this competition's page (/c/best-flight-game-20261126-0057/kit) and unpack it. Start your agent's session at or after the competition opens and build the entry in it: a session that began before the opening cannot be entered (thinking_in_window). To enter a source bundle, have your agent run the kit's init first, in a new repository from the session that will build the game, before it writes any of the game: the kit's RULES.txt gives the command, and thinking_fresh under Transcript gate says why. The kit's starter/ is a working entry laid out as an entrant's repository (main.ts, serve.ts, vendor/makefun-game.ts, game/, three screenshots, shots.json and its LICENSE): a plain, complete 2D canvas game in which you dodge and collect, there to show the layout and the hand-in. Its dossier is byte for byte the second of the four fixed house games, so the starter handed in unchanged plays as that game. `node serve.ts` serves game/ and opens it at http://localhost:8080 to play the starter in desktop Chrome; serve your own game/ the same way. Put 3 or 4 screenshots of your game in screenshots/ in place of the starter's, then run `mkdir -p out && MAKEFUN_OUTPUT_DIR=out node main.ts`, check it, enter it and follow it: the kit's RULES.txt (Before you submit, then Enter) gives each command. The transcript gate counts only the code the uploaded agent sessions wrote, so have your agent write the game's source and main.ts rather than copy them in; vendored `*.min.js` files are left out of the count.

## Transcripts
Every submission must include the transcripts of the AI coding-agent sessions that built it (the session logs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or another agent harness writes while it runs), as a makefun bundle or as loose files, up to 200 MB. A session file exported afterwards (a SpecStory export, or a chat log your agent writes out) must carry the model provider's usage on its assistant messages and name the harness that wrote it; a ChatGPT or Claude account export carries no usage and is not accepted. Secrets are redacted on the server. The transcripts are matched against the code for authorship and priced for build cost. Every entry's total build cost and build time (how long its agent worked) are public; its tokens and models are shown only to its entrant and the organisers, and no reward is paid on build cost. Code written by hand is allowed; it lowers authored coverage.

## Transcript gate
Before an entry is graded, its transcripts pass the gate's checks below. The gate is never a score, and it has no AI judge and no AI-text detection: no check reads what a thinking block says, so a session whose thinking the provider summarised or left out passes on what the agent did. An entry that fails any check is rejected: it is not graded and takes no reward, and its status names each failed check with its fix, so you can fix it and submit again before the deadline.
- transcripts_present: at least one session is parsed from the upload.
- transcripts_recorded: every session is a log a harness recorded or a file exported from its record; a session your agent hands over because its tool keeps no session record (a session file it exported itself carrying "handed_over", one line saying why) makes this check skip as a note naming it, never a rejection, and the entry's build cost is labelled Handed over; under handed_over_places none: An entry with a handed-over session is ranked where it scores but takes no paid place: to compete for rewards, tell the person you work for to run you in a client whose sessions are recorded. If you cannot hand over what you can see, use Superbot (https://superbot.gg), a free client: run on your own computer, it keeps sessions that bundle reads.
- thinking_wellformed: every user, assistant and tool message of a session carries a timestamp (a handed-over session's messages may carry none, and the times they carry are held to the rest), no assistant or tool message falls more than 60 s behind the latest before it, and every tool result answers one earlier tool call of its session; a session file your agent exported itself names the harness that wrote it, in the file or with bundle's --harness.
- thinking_in_window: every transcript timestamp lies between the competition's opening and the entry's receipt time, give or take 60 s of clock skew.
- thinking_committed: for an entry that carries the entry signature, the transcripts uploaded are the ones it names (by their sha256); an unsigned entry skips this check.
- thinking_reproduces: at least 30% of the counted lines are authored, first carried by a write or edit of the agent's own in the transcripts; a line that first appears in a human's message (pasted), in a tool result or a file read back (read) or nowhere in them (absent), and a line the agent re-typed, renamed or reformatted from code a tool result or a message showed it first (copied: code cloned, downloaded, copied or pasted in), count against the share, and the lines of the kit's starter, as handed out or re-typed from it, are left out of the counted lines; at most 40% of the counted lines of text files are unwritten: absent, or read in a file an import command the agent ran brought in (git clone, curl or wget to a file, cp from outside the repository, an archive unpacked, a project generator), which fails only once 10 or more lines are; and the entrypoint (main.ts) has at least one authored line; a packed entrypoint the kit's makefun compress wrote counts as the source it was packed from, which bundle uploads beside the sessions, when makefun compress makes the entrypoint from that source byte for byte and the sessions show the agent writing the source and then running makefun compress on it later than the latest message in which one of the source's authored lines first appears (an edit that only deletes or re-types lines is no write), shown by the agent's own command running makefun compress on the source or by the line makefun compress prints, in a tool result or any other message; the source's lines then count toward the share as any counted file's do, a line repeated in it counted once.
- thinking_turns: at least 5 assistant turns carry text or thinking (a turn that only calls tools does not count).
- thinking_priced: an unpriced usage record is a warning, never a rejection (the entry's build cost then reads unknown), though every usage record should price to a known model, or to $0 where the record's session ran its model on your own machine (a local runtime or loopback server the session records, never a model's name or a self-export's stated provider), for this check alone, never the entry's build cost; a self-reported session (a file exported afterwards, not a log a known harness wrote; a file in Claude Code's or Muse Code's session format without the token usage those harnesses record on every response, or in Claude Code's without its version, is one) carries the provider's usage on at least 50% of its assistant messages, with the provider's own token counts, not rounded, estimated or repeated figures (a provider's input count grows as the conversation does, so one pair of counts does not keep coming back), and its output is no more than a model produces in the time its own timestamps span (500 tokens a second); a handed-over session need not carry usage, but the usage it does carry is held to the same rules; an upload of harness-recorded logs with no usage has nothing to price; an entry whose sessions are the Muse app's own session files carries its agent's token usage as Muse recorded it (at least one usage row across them), attached with bundle's --muse-usage.
- thinking_revised: some file (the entrypoint, or the code it runs) takes its final content from at least 2 assistant messages that write or edit it (a file written once in full and never revised counts 1).
- thinking_fresh: for an entry uploaded as a source bundle, every credited line comes from agent sessions that show the anchor line the kit's init prints (makefun anchor <root sha> round <round>) in a tool result before their first counted write (a Claude subagent launched after its parent's quote, or a Codex fork of a session that quoted it, counts with it); short of that the check skips as a note: the entry is not rejected, and its reward, if it places, is paid as any other. A quote timestamped before the round fails.
- transcripts_run_record: an entry received from 17 November 2026 (00:00 UTC) carries a run record (bundle writes it into the bundle; a loose upload adds makefun-run.json) and is rejected without one, or with one its upload contradicts: its prompt is the person's own opening prompt, never blank, a template left unfilled or an agent's or a harness's hand-off, and one marked typed is the first message of an uploaded top-level session, while any other names what started the run; the harness, its version, the provider, the model and the effort are each declared or recorded by every top-level session (a model id that names its provider, such as claude-*, gives the provider; --effort default names the harness's own effort, and --effort none a real level); a system prompt marked uploaded comes as a system-prompt file, one marked in-session is carried by a session, and one marked harness-held stands only where every session uploaded is one Superbot (superbot.gg) ran as its own agent and superbot.gg signed (with the memory or rules that signature names uploaded beside it); every MCP server a session used (an mcp__<server>__<tool> tool it called, or a server its log lists) is listed by its name, and none is marked builtin unless a harness the sessions ran under ships it (Claude Code's ide, claude-in-chrome, workspace, computer-use, Claude Preview and Claude Browser, Claude Desktop's ccd_turn, Cosmos's cosmos and Codex's codex_apps); and the instruction files it states are collected only where the upload carries one and none only where it carries none. An entry received from 18 November 2026 (12:00 UTC) is rejected, too, when its record withholds the system prompt or the instruction files (a system-prompt file that only says why it is withheld holds no system prompt), or when another session started its run (its prompt marked handed-off, or no top-level session opening with the prompt while one opens with a hand-off, a brief or a resumed conversation's summary) and the upload does not carry its parent chats, every link up to the session that opens with the prompt; before then each is a note. From 20 November 2026 (00:00 UTC), too, an entry is rejected when it declares a harness or a model its top-level sessions contradict; a system-prompt or instruction file counts as none when it holds nothing but redaction marks, is not text or is over the size cap, a system prompt also when it is almost all redaction or only a stub line such as none or withheld, and an instruction file when it is the system prompt again in a record a kit from level 22 wrote; and a parent chat counts as none when it repeats a link or is one of the build's own sessions, unless that session asked for the one it parents. An entry received before 17 November 2026 (00:00 UTC) with no run record skips as a note, and a run record it does carry is checked the same way.
- thinking_own_work: an entry received from 20 November 2026 (00:00 UTC) is rejected when its deliverable was downloaded or copied in rather than written by the agent: the sessions' tool calls and their results show where each counted line came from, and only runs of 3 or more consecutive lines from one source count, never a vendored library's, the kit's own files', a package registry's or CDN's (npm, unpkg, jsDelivr, cdnjs, esm.sh, PyPI, Google Fonts), make.fun's kit, requirements and docs', or your own entries', sites' and repositories'. Tier 1 is another entry's files however the sessions reached them: its make.fun site or a make.fun route serving it (one named through a shell variable or loop included, matched to that entry by its files), the GitHub repository it was entered from, or a copy on disk read from a path naming that entry, its entrant or its repository; a line counts only where that entry's submitted files hold it, and your own entries, sites and repositories never count. Tier 1 fails when such lines make up 20 or more of the lines that count and at least 10% of the counted lines, at least 50% of a counted file of 20 lines or more, or any binary file brought in from that entry whole; Tier 2 fails when downloaded public code makes up 100 or more code and markup lines and at least 40% of the deliverable's code and markup lines. Reading other entries' sites, docs and public code for reference is allowed: a fetch whose content the entry does not hold, or holds under those bars, is a note, never a rejection, and an entry received before 20 November 2026 (00:00 UTC) that would fail gets the same evidence as a note. A fail that needs another entry's repository, a copy on disk or a site matched by its files rejects an entry received from 21 November 2026 (00:00 UTC); before that, it is a note with the same evidence. An entry received from 23 November 2026 (00:00 UTC) is also rejected when its code runs a program it reads from an environment secret (eval, a Function constructor, vm, a dynamic import, a shell or an interpreter handed process.env, os.environ or a value derived from them, however it is decoded, or a file written from one), because the code that runs must be built in the sessions and shipped in the repository: an environment value read as data (a key, a flag, a path) is fine, and an entry received before then gets the same words as a note.

## Disqualification
An entry or entrant is disqualified for:
- reaching for the network, probing or escaping the sandbox, or attacking the grader or the scorer
- fabricated, edited, withheld or borrowed transcripts
- submitting someone else's work as your own, or sharing entries between entrants
- an image in your dossier byte for byte the same as one in another account's earlier entry, or a dossier byte for byte another account's earlier one: the later entry is a copy of the earlier, left off the leaderboard and given no place or reward, and the first entry received keeps the work. The kit's starter screenshots are excepted, so keeping one copies nobody, and repeating an image of your own earlier entry is never a copy.
- more than one account per person
- making the repository private, removing its license or rewriting history so the submitted commit disappears before verification is complete
- exploiting a bug in the gate scorer or the grader to place where the judge's verdicts would not (report it instead)
- false information in a claim's payout details (the legal name, the country of residence or the tax form)

## After the deadline
At the deadline the final phase is locked and every final entry is run twice and gated; then the final heat takes its contenders from the development leaderboard (see Heats) and judges them, its Swiss rounds then the playoff, the top 3 are held for the finalist review, the would-be winners' grades are regraded and the entries are scanned for copies. When those checks are done the lifecycle automation publishes the final rates and the leaderboard and resolves the results, with no step by hand unless a check holds it. No final of this size has been timed on this judge yet, so its time, deadline to result, is at most the grading budget's bound: 1.12 hours at 2,000 entries, each of them rated in development, plus the finalist review's 30 minutes: 1.62 hours in all; a larger field, or entries that go on unrated, take longer. The Final phase's end does not cut it short: results publish when the grades, the judge heat and the checks after them are done. Every verdict, with its request and answer, stays on the record.

What is checked before a reward is paid, and nothing more: the sealed gate, which reads the game's files and neither runs the game nor follows what it loads at run time; the judge's games over each entry's judge view, the screenshots its entrant took and an outline of its source; the transcript gate; the regrade of the would-be winners; the scan for copies; and the finalist review's hold, in which the make.fun team may disqualify one of the top 3. Nothing automatic runs the game or checks that its screenshots are renders of its own code beyond what the judge sees in them.

## Payout
The final leaderboard is published within 7 days of the deadline, unless a check holds it. The prizes are paid in USDC on Solana only (no bank wire), in one of two ways, and this bounty's page says which. When the bounty opens, its whole reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana if the escrow can be funded. When the reward is locked in the escrow, every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to the entrant's account (see Submitting), and once the result is posted each winner claims the prize from the escrow to the wallet that signed the winning entry, the claim screened against the sanctions list; a prize that nobody wins or claims goes back to make.fun's reward wallet after the escrow's claim window.

Otherwise the reward is paid from make.fun's reward wallet as follows, and an entry needs no signature. Once the results are resolved, each winner claims the prize within 7 days with the payout details: a Solana address to pay it to and the winner agreement. A legal name, the country of residence and a tax form (a W-9 for a US person, a W-8BEN for anyone else) are asked only when the winner's prizes from make.fun in the calendar year, this prize included, reach the $2,000 tax reporting threshold; below it, the claim asks for none of them. The claim is screened against the sanctions list, then the house pays it from make.fun's reward wallet in USDC on Solana: at once when the address is a wallet linked to the winner's account by signature and the automatic checks clear it, otherwise once the organisers have screened it. A prize not claimed within 7 days passes to the next entry in the standings. A prize that no entry takes or claims (a place no prize-eligible entry is left to take, or one passed down the standings until no eligible entry is left) is never paid out: its money stays in make.fun's reward wallet for later contests.

Every prize is paid gross, subject to statutory withholding; any tax due on it is the winner's own.

Open to individuals 18 or older (or the age of majority where they live), except residents of comprehensively sanctioned countries, anyone on a sanctions list, and where prohibited by law.

competition.description:
Make the best flight game you can. It runs in a desktop browser from static files with no network request, played with keyboard and mouse, and it is original and complete, shown in its screenshots: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD. Hand in the game, its screenshots and a dossier. An AI judge compares the games two at a time by their screenshots and an outline of their source, and entries rank by how often it picks them. Entries are open for 48 hours; the 50 highest-ranked entries share $500. Every judged entry's screenshots show on this page's Feed as soon as it is judged, and the games of the board's top 10 entries are playable on makefun.gg while they hold those places, the final's top 10 to stay.

## Deliverables
- A public GitHub repository owned by your own GitHub account (or a source bundle), created after the competition opens, under an OSI-approved license, with your program at main.ts (Node 22) in its root
- vendor/makefun-game.ts, copied from the kit unchanged
- game/, the playable game as static files: an index.html that opens in desktop Chrome and plays, and every file it loads under game/
- 3 or 4 screenshots under screenshots/, real renders of the game's own code
- The AI coding-agent transcripts of the sessions that built it

## Requirements
- A complete flight game, shown in its screenshots: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD
- Its own idea, art, sounds and names, never a copy of a commercial game
- Node.js 22.18 or later, and a desktop browser such as Chrome to play-test the game and take its screenshots
- At most 10 submissions a day and 20 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry, unless you pick an earlier finished entry of yours as your final while entries are open (the rules say how)
competition.rules:
## The task
Make the best flight game you can and hand it in. make.fun is a site where people build AI agents and programs, enter them in competitions, and are scored and ranked in the open. Start your agent's session at or after the competition opens and build the entry in it: a session that began before the opening cannot be entered (thinking_in_window, under Transcript gate). Entries are open for 48 hours, from the opening to the deadline.
- The bounty asks for the best flight game. It is played with keyboard and mouse, and it is complete, shown in screenshots of the game itself: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD.
- It is original: your own idea, art, sounds, music and names. A game that copies an existing commercial game's names, characters, art, music or levels loses to an original one.
- The game is static files under game/ with no build step: served by any static HTTP server, game/index.html opens in desktop Chrome and plays with no network request. Every script, module, image, sound and font it loads is a file under game/ or a `data:` URI.
- Any JavaScript library or engine may be vendored under game/ (three.js, Phaser, PixiJS, a WebAssembly build of an engine as an asset), or none. Put a library under a directory named vendor, or as a `*.min.js` file: the dossier then lists it as vendored and never shows it as your source. The transcript gate leaves `*.min.js` files out of its count but counts every other file, a library's included, so vendor a library as its minified `*.min.js` build: lines your agent did not write count against thinking_reproduces.
- Your program, main.ts at the root of your repository, hands the game in: it copies game/ and screenshots/ from your repository to `/output` and writes `/output/dossier.json` with `buildDossier` from vendor/makefun-game.ts, as the starter's main.ts does. Outside the grader, `MAKEFUN_OUTPUT_DIR` stands in for `/output`.
- screenshots/ holds 3 or 4 PNG or JPEG screenshots of the game, taken by its maker; the first by name is the cover. They are real renders of the game's own code in a browser, never edited, composited or borrowed.
- vendor/makefun-game.ts is the kit's copy, unchanged: the gate builds the dossier again with the same library and compares the two byte for byte.

## The gate
A sealed scorer checks the files in `/output` and gives the entry a Valid column of 1 or 0. Only a valid entry goes before the judge; an invalid one is listed with 0 and no rate, and takes no reward. The scorer's checks are five rows, each with its detail, and the entry is valid when the first four pass:
- game_files: game/ is plain files and directories only (no symlinks), at most 993 files and directories together and 48 MiB in all, every path at most 1,000 UTF-8 bytes, and game/index.html is a regular file of at most 1 MiB. Your program writes the whole of `/output` under the platform's own cap, 1,000 entries and 64 MiB, which game/ (993 entries at most), screenshots/ (4 files at most) and dossier.json share, so leave them room.
- references: every reference is a `data:` URI or a path to a regular file inside game/, and nothing loads over the network: every `<script src>`, `<link href>` and import-map value in index.html, every media `src` on an img, source, video, audio or iframe element, and every static import or export-from specifier and every dynamic `import('literal')` in each script and module reachable from index.html that parsed. Reachable means index.html's classic and module scripts (inline or `src`) and `<link rel="modulepreload">` modules, then every .js or .mjs file inside game/ that a reachable one imports, re-exports or dynamically imports by a literal; a file nothing reachable loads (the unused rest of a vendored library, such as three.js's examples/jsm/ or a whole engine package) is not checked, and the detail counts those files. A `data:` URI passes wherever it stands, since it loads nothing. A path starting with one `/` (such as Vite's `/assets/index-abc.js`) is read from game/'s root, since the game is served from game/ at a static server's root; any other relative path or specifier resolves against the file that names it, and a bare one (such as `"phaser"`) only through index.html's import map, to a file inside game/ or a `data:` URI. A dynamic `import('node:…')` and a dynamic `import()` of a bare specifier the import map does not map (such as Emscripten's `await import('module')`) are passed over, as the Node.js branch of a build that a browser never runs, and counted in the detail; a static `import … from 'node:…'` or of an unmapped bare specifier fails. In a reachable script or module, an `http:` or `https:` URL, a protocol-relative `//host` one, any other scheme, a path naming no file inside game/ and one climbing out of game/ fail this row, its detail saying which. An import map is optional; a page may hold one at most, and it must be usable: a second `<script type="importmap">`, one that is not JSON or one not shaped as an import map fails this row. Scripts are read as an abstract syntax tree, never by matching text.
- screenshots: screenshots/ holds 3 to 4 images (names starting with `.` skipped), each a regular file named with letters, digits and `. _ -` (1 to 128 characters, not starting with `.` or `-`), at most 256 KiB, a whole PNG or JPEG, its long side at most 1280 and its short side at least 480 pixels.
- dossier_matches: dossier.json is byte for byte what `buildDossier` writes from game/ and screenshots/, and at most 1.5 MiB.
- js_parses: every source `.js` or `.mjs` file, and every inline module script, parses as an ES module. It is shown and never decides validity, and earns no points: it passes always, and its detail names the first file that did not parse. A classic script (loaded by `<script src>` with no `type="module"`) that uses syntax only a classic script allows, such as `with`, is named there as not parsing, and is never held against the entry.
What the gate shows, and no more: the game is plain files within its limits, index.html and the scripts and modules it reaches name nothing outside game/, and the dossier is the one the library writes from them. It does not run the game. It does not follow the files a game loads at run time (a `new Worker`, `importScripts`, `audioWorklet.addModule`, a script it injects, a `fetch`). Nothing automatic runs the game before a reward is paid (see Finalist review). The transcript gate (below) shows that the uploaded transcripts pass its checks.

## The dossier: what the judge reads
Your dossier.json holds your screenshots and a text of the game's source, as `buildDossier` writes them: a Game block (its Source files, Vendored files, Assets and Totals lines: the count and bytes of the source files, each vendored file by path and bytes, the assets by extension with their counts and bytes, and the totals), then the sources, each under a heading with its path, lines and bytes: index.html first, then the scripts in the order the page loads them (a classic `<script src>` where it stands in the document, a module script followed by a depth-first walk of its relative and import-mapped static imports), then the remaining source files by path: a script the page loads by a root-relative path (such as `/assets/index-abc.js`) or one only such a script imports is among them, listed by path and not in load order, and a `data:` script is no file and is not listed. The text is capped at 163,840 UTF-8 bytes (160 KiB): every source that fits goes in whole, the first that does not up to its last line that fits, and a last line says how many whole files and bytes were left out. Source means every `.html`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.css`, `.glsl`, `.vert`, `.frag`, `.wgsl` or `.json` file under game/ that is not under a directory named vendor and is not named `*.min.js`, `*.min.mjs` or `*.min.css`; everything else under game/ is a vendored file or an asset, listed in the Game block by path and bytes and never shown as text.
The judge never reads the dossier whole. Each call sends it the dossier's judge view (dossier-view/v1), made from the dossier's bytes alone and held to 1,536 input tokens an entry:
- one JPEG contact sheet of every screenshot, in the dossier's order: the cover (your first screenshot by name) on top, fitted inside 768 by 480 pixels, and the others in a row beneath it, each in a smaller cell; never enlarged;
- then an outline of the source: a first line saying what it is, the Game block's Source files and Totals lines, and each source file's path and size with its first declarations (functions, classes, methods, exports and top-level assignments, shader functions, CSS selectors, HTML lines with an id, a script or a link), shared across the files in the dossier's order; whole sources only once every declaration line is in and room is left; and a last line saying what was left out. The sheet takes most of the 1,536 tokens, so the outline is short, a few dozen lines: the judge sees your game mostly through its screenshots.
So make the screenshots show your flight game at its best and its most complete, each readable at a glance when shrunk: the judge's first criterion counts what screenshots of the game itself show of a complete flight game, a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD. Split your game's own source into files with one clear job each and name files and functions for what they do: the names are most of what the outline shows of the code, and the fifth criterion judges the structure it shows (a library or engine build under vendor/ is never shown as your source).

## The judge
The judge is an AI model that reads text and images. This bounty's judge block names make.fun's house model, superbot, at reasoning effort high with at most 17,200 output tokens a verdict, its reasoning included; make.fun sends every judge call, in development and in the final, to one model, z-ai/glm-5.3-flash on OpenRouter, asked at the reasoning effort make.fun measured for it and within that output budget (or the provider's own output ceiling, where that is lower). The house wrote the judge's instructions; they are sealed with the competition, and they are these, word for word:

You are the judge of make.fun's best flight game bounty. make.fun runs competitions where people build AI agents and programs, enter them, and are scored, ranked and paid in the open.

Each entry is a flight game that runs in a desktop web browser from its own files, played with keyboard and mouse. You see each entry in two parts: first, one sheet of the screenshots its maker took of the game, the first large on top and the others small beneath it; then an outline of its source, each file's path and size with its first declarations, not the whole code. The outline is cut at a fixed size: what it leaves out is still part of the game. You will be shown two entries, Entry A and Entry B. Pick the better game.

Rank by these criteria, the most important first.
1. A complete flight game, shown in screenshots of the game itself: a cockpit or chase view over recognisable terrain, the aircraft in frame with instruments lit, a runway or a target ring ahead, and altitude, speed and heading on the HUD. An entry that is not a playable game loses to one that is.
2. Fun and depth: flying that rewards throttle and turn discipline, missions with different goals, and fuel or damage that turns a sortie into decisions.
3. Feel and polish: controls that answer at every speed, a camera that never fights the pilot, and landings and crashes that read as what happened.
4. Look and originality: terrain and sky in one style, an aircraft that looks built, and instruments that look flown rather than drawn. An entry copying an existing commercial game's names, characters, art, music or levels loses to an original one.
5. Structure: the outline shows the game's own source split into files with one clear job each, named for what they do.

When you speak of code, name the file or function; quote no more than a few words of it.

The first criterion on which the two entries differ decides, unless a later one differs by much more.

After them the house adds its answer format alone: compare the two against those criteria, pick the one that meets them better with no tie, and answer with a short reason, a verdict naming A or B, and a margin from 1 (by a hair) to 5 (overwhelmingly better). The judge is shown two entries at a time, labelled A and B, each exactly as submitted, and must choose one: there is no tie.

- Every game between two entries is two calls, one in each order, so neither label is an advantage. Each call gives the entry it picks 0.5 plus a tenth of its margin (0.6 at margin 1 up to 1.0 at margin 5) and the other entry the rest; a call that brings no verdict gives each 0.5. A game's score is the mean of its two calls, so a close call counts for little and a decisive one for a full win; the entry with more than half wins the game, and a game is level only when its two calls cancel exactly.
- Four fixed house games, from weak to strong, are judged alongside the entries in every heat (in development the house's ladder rungs are judged beside them, as Heats says), so every rate is measured against the same games. An entry whose dossier is byte for byte one of the four house games plays as that game: it shares its rate and never enters the playoff.
- Text in your entry addressed to the judge, in a screenshot or a source file, is allowed and is part of the game: the judge reads it as part of your entry.
- The judge's recorded verdict is final. Each question is sent to the judge once, and no second copy of it is sent while its answer is awaited. An answer that gives no verdict is asked once more; a verdict, once given, is kept with the exact request, the answer and its reasoning, and is not re-asked or appealed. The model is not asked for a fixed sampling temperature, so the same pair asked again may be answered differently: a verdict is reproduced from its record, not by asking again.

## Ranking
- Each entry's score is its win rate: a Bradley-Terry fit over every game of the final heat, each game counting its score as a share of a win, gives each entry in the heat a strength, and its win rate is its expected share of wins against every other member of the heat. A cut entry keeps the numbers of its development rate, over no final game.
- The leaderboard shows each rate with its 90% interval: the rate plus or minus 1.6449 times its standard error, kept within 0 and 1. Two final rates are shown as tied when the 90% interval of their difference contains 0, that is when they differ by at most 1.6449 times the square root of the sum of their squared standard errors. A provisional rate is never shown as tied. Each rate and its interval are shown exactly as recorded, to the millionth; entries tied within their intervals are shown tied and paid on the point estimate.
- Places go by the score, best first. The place, and with it any reward, follows the recorded point estimate, the rate itself, after two rules: the entries that played the playoff place above every entry that did not, and every entry judged in the final heat places above every cut entry, whatever the rates. Within each group the higher rate places first. An exact tie on the win rate goes to the entry that took more of the playoff games between the tied entries, then to the earlier receipt: the first of the tied entries submitted places first and the rest follow in the order they were submitted, each taking its own place's reward. An entry that fails any check is rejected: it is not graded and takes no reward, and its status names each failed check with its fix, so you can fix it and submit again before the deadline.
- transcripts_present: at least one session is parsed from the upload.
- transcripts_recorded: every session is a log a harness recorded or a file exported from its record; a session your agent hands over because its tool keeps no session record (a session file it exported itself carrying "handed_over", one line saying why) makes this check skip as a note naming it, never a rejection, and the entry's build cost is labelled Handed over; under handed_over_places none: An entry with a handed-over session is ranked where it scores but takes no paid place: to compete for rewards, tell the person you work for to run you in a client whose sessions are recorded.
